method: Read all seven full bilingual P-v2 bodies and current canonical goals; checked direct BY/HE/BW source contexts, all seven current image hashes against the active chemistry AI visualization-QA ledger, and actual original images for 42a84bca, 13d4f336 and 78109f6d. Opened and identified the cited DGUV PDF itself and compared relevant official DGUV school/first-aid publications. Content/source HOLDs are independent of the technical checker.

targetedCheck.result: Technical PASS: configured 7, blocking issues 0, needs human review 7, approved 0.

decisions.finding: The O2/H2O/Cl2 and H2O+CO2 examples are individually classified correctly and fit the direct BY C8.3.3 element/compound/mixture clause. The essential understanding, however, universally defines a pure substance as one particle species and a compound as chemically bound atom species. A pure ionic compound such as NaCl has Na+ and Cl− ion species in one lattice; its purity is one substance/fixed composition, not literally one molecular or ionic particle type. The molecular-example image uses the same simplified caption, so the corrected P must identify its model scope rather than repeating it as a universal law. The image itself was not changed or newly V-approved by this P review.
decisions.requiredResolution: Qualify one-particle-species language as applying to the depicted atomic/molecular examples, give a chemically general pure-substance definition, and keep ionic compounds in scope without inventing discrete salt molecules. Recheck the affected P body and page-image context.

decisions.finding: The supplied-card acid-splash and fresh volatile-vapor cases distinguish substance hazard from route/amount/procedure-dependent exposure risk. Eye protection, small quantities, teacher control and ventilation/closure address the specified routes. Neither case asks a learner to handle a hazardous substance. This concretizes the canonical risk-minimization goal and HE 8.1 hazard labeling/protection context without claiming that a symbol itself grants permission.

decisions.bodyFinding: The supervised water-only preparation case tests actual safe action, not memorized rules. The separate paper splash case addresses immediate stop/teacher alert, possible skin and clothing contamination, prompt skin rinsing, contaminated-clothing removal with help, local first-aid response and no improvised neutralization. This is broadly compatible with school chemical first-aid guidance; the active generic safety image does not itself depict first aid and is not used as proof of mastery.
decisions.blockingSourceFinding: The v3 candidate reason cites DGUV article/1358 as information for skin contact and contaminated clothing. The actual PDF is DGUV Regel 101-019, 'Umgang mit Reinigungs- und Pflegemitteln', issued for building-cleaning work, not school chemistry. That link does not substantiate the claimed school-lab context. School-specific DGUV Regel 113-018 section III-2.1 explicitly treats classroom chemical accidents, contaminated clothing and prompt water rinsing; DGUV Information 204-022 p.82 separately supports clothing removal and thorough water rinsing for toxic/corrosive skin exposure. The source claim must be corrected substantively, not just given a new hash.
decisions.requiredResolution: Replace the cleaning-products citation with an accurately identified school chemical first-aid source and keep the response wording within what that source supports; rematerialize/recheck the affected current P record.

decisions.finding: Water phase-change diagrams conserve H2O molecules rather than enlarging or decomposing them. The fresh I2 sublimation error case conserves I2, changes spacing/motion and correctly identifies energy uptake. This stays within the split BW 3.2.1.2 (3) state-change clause; no chemical reaction is asserted.

The two cases deliberately distinguish dissolved sugar molecules from separated Na+/Cl− ions in salt solution, conserve solute components and explain why clear solution passes ordinary paper filtration. No hands-on salt experiment is required. This fits the split BW solution-process modeling clause.

The still-water bead track and spreading dye distinguish Brownian motion of one suspended particle from net diffusion of many molecules. Fresh scent/fan data add a directed-flow control and avoid calling bulk airflow pure diffusion. This matches the split BW 3.2.1.2 (3) diffusion/Brownian clause.

The salt-solution case separates observed clarity from an inferred ion model. The independent closed-bag vinegar/baking-soda data show gas formation with unchanged total mass and require correcting a particle sketch without disappearing C/O atoms; no full equation or hands-on experiment is demanded. The active sugar image illustrates the level distinction but is not treated as learner evidence.
